title: Firework Painting
strapline: Bright paint flicked and blown across dark paper — the bang and sparkle of a firework, made safely indoors.
intent: Children explore colour, sound and movement as a way of celebrating Bonfire Night and New Year.
Children gain vivid descriptive vocabulary — bang, sparkle, whoosh, bright — from a real sensory experience.
Blowing, flicking and dabbing are expressive art techniques that also build breath control and coordination.
Working on dark paper flips children's expectations of what paint does, which is a provocation in itself.
Sharing a limited set of tools builds turn-taking at a busy, exciting table.
implementation: Set out black or dark paper with bright, well-loaded paints in shallow trays.
Offer several techniques — straws to blow with, toothbrushes to flick, pom-poms to dab.
Demonstrate each technique once, then let children combine them however they like.
Expect and plan for mess: aprons, floor covering, and a table children can lean right over.
Talk the vocabulary as they work — bang, sparkle, fizz, shower, bright, glittering.
Play firework sounds or music quietly to connect the mark to the memory.
Support turn-taking with the straws and brushes rather than providing one of everything.
key_questions: What happens to the paint when you blow hard, and when you blow gently?
What sound would your firework make?
Which colours show up best on the dark paper?
How could you make your firework look like it is exploding?
What do you remember about seeing real fireworks?

impact.text: Children gain and use vivid descriptive vocabulary from a real experience.
Children make deliberate choices about colour, tool and technique.
Children improve coordination and control using tools in a new way.
Children talk about their own picture and notice detail in their friends' work.
Children share limited resources and take turns at a busy table.
Children recount a real event — seeing fireworks — in rough sequence.

enhancements: A large collaborative firework mural the whole room contributes to.
Glitter, foil and sequins added once the paint is dry for a second layer.
A sound table with shakers and drums to make the firework noises.
A ribbon-and-scarf dancing session moving like a firework going up and falling.
A safety conversation about sparklers and bonfires, led by children's own questions.
A dark-room display with torches so the paintings can be viewed as if at night.

playing_exploring: Children experiment freely with what blowing and flicking will do.
Unfamiliar tools on unfamiliar paper invite pure investigation.
active_learning: Children repeat and refine a technique until the effect is what they wanted.
The excitement holds their attention through a long, messy task.
creating_thinking: Children predict and test what each tool will do to the paint.
They connect the marks they make to a firework they have actually seen.
